passage:
Paragraph A
An octopus resting on a coral head can vanish before your eyes. In less than a second its skin runs through a shifting palette of browns, yellows and greens until it matches the rock beneath it, complete with imitation lumps and shadows. Cuttlefish and squid, the octopus's close relatives in the group known as the cephalopods, are equally gifted. Their control of colour is faster and far more elaborate than that of the chameleon, the animal most people think of first when quick colour change is mentioned. A chameleon may take several seconds to shift its hue; a cuttlefish can repaint its entire body several times a second.

Paragraph B
What makes this ability so puzzling is that most cephalopods appear to be colour-blind. Their eyes contain only a single type of light-sensitive pigment, so in the ordinary sense they cannot tell red from green. Yet somehow they produce patterns that match the colours, and not merely the brightness, of their surroundings. How an animal that cannot see colour manages to imitate it so precisely is one of the enduring questions of marine biology, and the answer lies less in the eye than in the remarkable structure of the skin itself.

Paragraph C
The uppermost of the skin's working layers is packed with tiny organs called chromatophores. Each chromatophore is an elastic sac holding a grain of pigment — yellow, red, brown or black — and is ringed by a set of muscles. When the muscles contract, they stretch the sac outward into a flat disc of colour many times the area of its resting spot; when they relax, the sac springs back to an almost invisible dot. Crucially, these muscles are wired directly to the animal's brain by nerves rather than being switched on slowly by hormones in the blood. It is this direct nervous control that gives the cephalopod its extraordinary speed.

Paragraph D
Beneath the chromatophores lies a second layer built from cells called iridophores. Iridophores contain no pigment at all. Instead they are made of stacks of ultra-thin plates that bend and reflect light, so that particular wavelengths are cancelled or reinforced as they bounce between the layers. This is the same physical effect — interference — that produces the colours of a soap bubble or a peacock's feather, and in cephalopods it generates the blues and greens that pigment alone cannot make. In some species the spacing of the plates can even be adjusted, tuning the reflected colour from moment to moment.

Paragraph E
A third layer, deeper still, contains leucophores. These cells scatter every wavelength of light equally and so appear a flat, bright white whatever the colour of the light falling on them. A leucophore therefore behaves like a sheet of white paper held behind the coloured layers above: it reflects back whatever ambient light reaches it, and this broadband mirror helps the animal take on the general tone of its background. Together the three layers — pigment, interference and scatter — give the skin a range of effects that no single mechanism could achieve.

Paragraph F
Controlling all of this is a nervous system of astonishing reach. A large cuttlefish carries several million chromatophores, and each is linked to motor neurons in the brain that can be fired independently. Biologists have found that the animal does not command every spot one at a time. Instead it assembles its appearance from a limited set of pattern ‘components’ — a uniform tone, a fine mottle, a bold disruptive blotch — which are layered and combined much as a printer builds an image from a few inks. This economical system is what allows a response fast enough to fool a passing predator.

Paragraph G
Camouflage is only part of the story. Cephalopods also use their skin to signal. Male cuttlefish court females with rippling waves of colour, and a courting male swimming beside a rival has been seen to split its display down the middle: it shows tender courtship patterns on the side facing the female while presenting drab, female-like camouflage on the side facing the competitor, so as not to provoke him. There is also growing evidence that the skin itself may sense light. Light-sensitive proteins of the kind normally found in eyes have been detected in the skin of several species, hinting that a cephalopod might, in a limited way, ‘see’ with its whole body.

Paragraph H
The study of these animals has consequences far beyond the aquarium. Engineers designing flexible electronic displays and adaptive camouflage fabrics have begun to copy the layered logic of cephalopod skin, in which colour is produced by controlling light rather than by printing fixed dyes. For neuroscientists, meanwhile, the cephalopod offers a rare gift: a nervous system whose decisions are written out, instantly and visibly, across the animal's own body. To watch a cuttlefish change colour is, in a sense, to watch it think.
